Chapter 5: Meaning, Morality, and Awe Without Supernatural Belief
You know, there’s this really common worry that if you stop believing in a supernatural God, life just sort of... loses its spark. People wonder—does morality turn into a free-for-all? Does our sense of awe fade away, replaced by cynicism? But let’s pause for a second—because that fear actually misses where meaning and morality truly come from.
Picture a young adult, just stepping out into the world on their own. Suddenly, every decision—career, relationships, what really matters—is all up to them. The old guardrails are gone, and the future feels like a big question mark. It’s tempting to float along, letting life happen. But as time goes on, something becomes clear...
Meaning isn’t something handed down from above. It’s something you build, piece by piece, with every choice you make and every commitment you keep.
Think about where most people find purpose: it’s in connection—with family, with friends, with causes that stretch beyond just ourselves. These bonds aren’t gifts from the divine. They’re the product of our evolutionary story. Social animals survive by cooperating, by looking out for each other, by building communities that last. So if you look for the roots of morality, you’ll find them deep in the natural world.
Imagine a volunteer, giving up their weekends to help out at a local shelter. They’re not doing it because they’re afraid of punishment or chasing some heavenly reward—they do it because it feels right. That deep sense of fulfillment? It doesn’t come from following orders from a higher power. It comes from the simple act of making a difference. That urge to help, to care, to create something beautiful or bring a little order to the chaos—it’s as natural as needing to sleep or eat.
And here’s something a lot of people overlook: awe and reverence don’t need the supernatural. Think about standing at the foot of a mountain, or witnessing the birth of a child, or even just marveling at the intricate complexity of a single cell. That sense of wonder doesn’t need any explanation beyond the moment itself. To stand in the presence of the universe—to feel both tiny and deeply connected at the same time—that’s experiencing the sacred, right in the ordinary.
And what about critical thinking, or questioning, or being open to new ideas? Far from taking away from spirituality, these are the things that actually ground it. Being willing to doubt, to ask new questions, to chase after understanding—that’s what makes the search for meaning real. The biggest questions—about why we’re here, what consciousness is, or what it really means to be good—aren’t solved once and for all. They’re lived, day by day, as we keep asking, keep learning, and keep growing.
